questions.question: What must be checked to show that a subspace U is invariant under a linear operator A?
options: Every vector in V is sent into U by A.
Every vector in U is fixed pointwise by A.
Every vector u in U is sent back into U by A.
Every vector outside U is sent to zero.

questions.question: Does an invariant subspace have to consist only of eigenvectors?
options: No. It only has to be closed under the action of A.
Yes, but only for diagonal matrices.
No. It does not even need to be a subspace.
Yes. Every nonzero vector in it must be an eigenvector.

questions.question: Why is the span of an eigenvector p invariant under A?
options: Because $Ap=λp$ remains in the same one-dimensional span.
Because $Ap=0$ for every eigenvector, and $0$ is in the span.
Because $Ap=p$, so $A$ leaves each eigenvector unchanged.
Because $\operatorname{span}(p)$ is the whole space $V$ when $p\neq0$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, is the line $span((1,1)^{\top})$ invariant?
options: No, A sends it to $(1,-1)^{\top}$.
Yes, A sends $(1,1)^{\top}$ to itself.
No, a line is invariant only for diagonal matrices.
Only if the scalar multiplying $(1,1)^{\top}$ is zero.

questions.question: If U is invariant under A, what does the restriction of A to U mean?
options: A maps U onto the whole space V, not into U.
A acts as the identity on every vector of U.
A sends each vector of U to a multiple of itself.
A can be viewed as an operator from U to U.

questions.question: Why is range A invariant under A for a linear operator A on V?
options: If y=Ax, then Ay must be zero.
Range A is invariant because every vector is in the kernel.
If y=Ax, then Ay=A(Ax), which is again an output of A.
Range A is invariant only when A is diagonalizable.

questions.question: Let A be rotation by 90 degrees in $R^2$. Is the x-axis invariant?
options: No, the x-axis is sent to the y-axis.
Yes, because rotations preserve lengths.
Yes, because the x-axis is a subspace.
Only if the vector has length 1.

questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=span((1,1)^{\top})$. Is U invariant?
options: Only if 2 and 3 are both nonzero.
Yes, because every one-dimensional subspace is invariant.
Yes, because A is diagonal.
No, because $A(1,1)^{\top}=(2,3)^{\top}$ is not a multiple of $(1,1)^{\top}$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}$ be a linear operator on $V$ and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ with $\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. When is the line $\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{p})$ invariant under $\boldsymbol{A}$?
options: Exactly when $\boldsymbol{p}$ is an eigenvector of $\boldsymbol{A}$
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{p}$
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{0}$
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}$ is orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{p}$

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}$ be a linear operator on $V$. Why is $\ker\boldsymbol{A}$ always invariant under $\boldsymbol{A}$?
options: For $\boldsymbol{u}\in\ker\boldsymbol{A}$, $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{0}$, which lies in $\ker\boldsymbol{A}$.
Every $\boldsymbol{u}\in\ker\boldsymbol{A}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{u}$, so it stays where it is.
$\ker\boldsymbol{A}$ always equals $\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}$, which contains every image.
It is invariant only when $\boldsymbol{A}$ is invertible, so $\ker\boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$.

questions.question: Let $U$ be the plane $z=0$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\boldsymbol{A}(x,y,z)=(x+y,\,y,\,2z)$. Is $U$ invariant under $\boldsymbol{A}$?
options: Yes: if $z=0$, the third coordinate of $\boldsymbol{A}(x,y,z)$ is also $0$.
No: $(0,1,0)$ is in $U$ but is not an eigenvector of $\boldsymbol{A}$.
No: $\boldsymbol{A}$ is not the identity on $U$.
No: the first coordinate changes from $x$ to $x+y$.
